job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based solely on the supplied text, these are the identifiable loopholes, ambiguities, and enforcement weaknesses. Some are clear exclusions; others are potential disputes, not established legal defects. Generally applicable law may fill some gaps, so an omitted provision does not necessarily mean an activity is lawful or enforcement is impossible.

### Definitions and scope

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel production threshold.** Companies could distribute recovery among multiple vessels, keeping each at or below 10,000 metric tons annually. There is no aggregation across a company, affiliated companies, a fleet, or a mining project, although a determination under section 2(1)(B) might reach those activities.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Exact numerical boundaries.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons annually, or mining at depths of exactly 200 meters or less, falls outside subparagraph (A). These are express exclusions, not necessarily drafting mistakes, and subparagraph (B) could potentially cover them.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual accounting period.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, a rolling 12-month period, or another reporting year. That uncertainty affects whether operators can concentrate recovery around year boundaries without crossing the threshold.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unspecified measurement method.** The text does not specify whether tonnage means wet material, dry nodules or ore, processed mineral content, or material including attached sediment. Different methods could substantially change whether an operation qualifies.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unclear attribution of recovery to a vessel.** The bill does not explain how to allocate recovery involving underwater robots, several support ships, transshipment, or fixed installations. Operators could dispute which vessel recovered the material—or whether recovery was “by a single vessel” at all.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unclear point of recovery and depth measurement.** “Recovery” could refer to extraction from the seabed, collection, lifting to the surface, or retention aboard a vessel, and the bill supplies no depth-measurement convention. Those omissions complicate proof for projects spanning the 200-meter boundary or using several extraction stages.

7. **Section 2(1)—Preparatory and supporting activities are not expressly covered.** Exploration, equipment installation, financing, transportation, processing, and purchasing are not independently prohibited. Whether particular conduct constitutes “engag[ing] in” mining, falls within subparagraph (B), or creates liability under generally applicable participation rules would require separate analysis.

8. **Section 2(1)—“Commercial” does not turn on commercial purpose.** Despite its label, the definition contains no requirement of sales, profit, or commercial intent. It could cover large scientific recoveries while excluding smaller profit-making operations under subparagraph (A), making the bill’s reach different from what its terminology suggests.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—Undefined decision-maker.** The Act never defines “the Secretary”; naming the Secretary of State separately in section 6 and NOAA in section 4 does not clearly assign this power. That omission creates a foundational dispute over who may expand the prohibition.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—Unspecified risk standard.** “Risks,” “comparable,” and the relevant ecosystem impacts are undefined, while the benchmark encompasses widely varying mining operations. The provision invites disputes over scientific evidence, consistency, and fair notice, especially when a determination supplies the basis for criminal liability.

11. **Section 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure or deadline.** The text does not specify whether determinations must be general rules or project-specific decisions, when they become operative, or how affected parties receive notice. Existing administrative-law requirements may apply, but the bill itself neither resolves these questions nor requires timely action against activities outside subparagraph (A).

12. **Section 2(1)(B)—Catchall potentially extends beyond seabed mining.** “Any activity” is not expressly limited by depth, mineral recovery, vessel size, or commercial purpose. That breadth could generate challenges to expansive applications and makes the prohibition’s outer boundary uncertain.

13. **Section 2(2)—Incomplete coverage of individuals abroad.** “U.S. person” includes citizens but not noncitizen U.S. nationals or lawful permanent residents as such. Those individuals’ activities abroad therefore do not automatically fall within section 3(a).

14. **Section 2(2)—Incomplete coverage of domestic entities abroad.** The definition names corporations but not partnerships, LLCs that are not corporations, trusts, or other entities. It also does not expressly include corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law, creating exclusions or interpretive disputes for their overseas activities.

15. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not automatically covered.** A foreign-incorporated company does not become a “U.S. person” merely because Americans own or control it. Covered parents or individuals could still face liability for their own participation, but the bill contains no express ownership, control, or anti-circumvention rule.

16. **Section 3(a)—Uncertain geographic reach of “in the United States.”** The phrase does not expressly address territories, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. In particular, U.S. resource jurisdiction offshore does not necessarily make those waters “in the United States,” leaving room for disputes involving foreign operators.

### Exemptions

17. **Section 3(b)—Exploration licenses can exempt mining.** The exception is framed around mining “under an exploration license,” without limiting the amount recovered or expressly excluding commercial production. Whether an exploration license actually authorizes particular mining would matter, but the wording risks protecting considerably more than exploration.

18. **Section 3(b)—No limit on qualifying license issuers.** The bill does not specify a U.S. agency, foreign government, or international authority as the required issuer. Operators could argue that a pre-enactment license from any qualifying authority triggers the exemption.

19. **Section 3(b)—Unclear treatment of transfers, renewals, and expansions.** The exception does not address changes in ownership, extensions, amendments, enlarged licensed areas, or increased production. Companies could acquire old licenses or argue that substantially altered operations remain protected by their original issuance dates.

20. **Section 3(b)—No requirement for actual existing operations.** Despite the heading, the operative language requires a pre-enactment license, not mining already underway. It could protect dormant projects and licenses obtained shortly before enactment, with no separate phaseout or production cap during the Act’s life.

21. **Section 3(c)—Environmental-assessment exception lacks safeguards.** There is no approval requirement, qualifying methodology, independent supervision, recovery limit, or obligation to publish findings. An operator could invoke environmental assessment to defend a substantial extraction program, although that claimed purpose could still be contested.

22. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The text does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, or prohibit selling recovered minerals. A project serving both assessment and commercial objectives could therefore claim the exception.

### Registry and enforcement

23. **Sections 2(3) and 4(a)—Registry excludes smaller mining vessels.** Only vessels exceeding 5,000 gross tons must register, regardless of their actual recovery capacity. Smaller vessels may still violate section 3, but their exclusion from the registry removes a monitoring mechanism; the bill also does not specify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement system.

24. **Sections 2(3) and 4(a)—“Equipped” and “operator” are undefined.** Registration coverage may be disputed for vessels using temporarily installed equipment, remotely operated collectors, or shared recovery systems. Unclear allocation of operator status among owners, charterers, and contractors also complicates accountability.

25. **Section 4(a)—Registry’s jurisdictional reach is unstated.** “Each covered vessel” is not limited by flag, location, ownership, or connection to the United States. A literal worldwide reading would raise jurisdictional and practical enforcement problems, while a narrower interpretation leaves uncertain which foreign vessels must register.

26. **Section 4—No registration deadline or detailed reporting requirements.** The bill does not say whether registration must precede operations or specify reporting due dates, tonnage fields, locations, license information, or record-retention duties. A report merely “describing” activities may be inadequate to establish violations or test claimed exemptions.

27. **Sections 4(b) and 5—Nonregistration and nonreporting lack express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not section 4, and reporting duties attach to “registered” operators. General false-statement law may address some knowingly false submissions, but the Act supplies no comparable explicit sanction for failing to register or report.

28. **Sections 3–5—Enforcement responsibility and procedures are incomplete.** NOAA receives registrations and reports, but the bill does not expressly designate who investigates violations or assesses civil penalties, or establish an administrative assessment process. Existing judicial and agency authorities may help, but the text leaves important institutional questions unresolved.

29. **Sections 4–5—No express verification or stop-work powers.** The bill does not specifically authorize inspections, vessel boarding, access to underlying records, subpoenas, or stop-work orders. Quarterly operator-certified reports alone would make detection difficult, and the availability of stronger measures would depend on other legal authority.

30. **Section 5(a)—Annual threshold conflicts with daily penalty calculation.** The bill does not explain whether exceeding 10,000 tons makes earlier recovery days violations, only subsequent days violations, or some other set of days. Nor does it clarify how to count an ongoing mining operation on days without actual recovery.

31. **Section 5—Penalties do not expressly recover economic gains.** The Act provides no specific forfeiture, disgorgement, or restoration remedy, and civil penalties have a ceiling but no minimum. The substantial daily maximum may deter violations, but the text does not ensure that enforcement eliminates their financial benefit.

32. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Conflicting commencement language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effective date by 180 days. The better reading may be that no section 3 violation exists before effectiveness, but the mismatch invites disputes over civil liability during that interval.

33. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 5(b)—Criminal application requires particular clarity.** Undefined boundaries and later agency determinations create potential fair-notice challenges when violations carry up to 10 years’ imprisonment. The “willfully” requirement supplies protection against some unfair applications, but its meaning and the required proof of knowledge would themselves matter.

### International provisions, duration, and implementation

34. **Section 6—Negotiation is not an enforceable international prohibition.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate,” not obtain an agreement, and the deadline does not clearly identify a required negotiating milestone. The provision supplies no fallback if talks fail and does not itself bind foreign companies.

35. **Section 6—“Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** It is unclear whether an agreement must reproduce section 3’s exemptions or merely achieve comparable restrictions. The bill also supplies no implementation or international compliance mechanism if an agreement is reached.

36. **Section 7(a)—Scientific review has no specified process.** No provision commissions or funds the National Academies report, sets a deadline, or defines “serious harm” and the conditions under which mining must be assessed. Congress therefore receives no clear statutory framework for evaluating a proposed early termination.

37. **Section 7(a)—Early termination may leave disconnected obligations.** The joint-resolution mechanism ends the section 3 prohibition, not expressly the registry and reporting provisions. Operators could remain subject to administrative requirements after mining becomes lawful under this Act.

38. **Section 7(b)—Automatic sunset overrides the scientific condition.** The entire Act expires after 10 years even without a favorable National Academies report or congressional finding. Mining would then no longer be prohibited by this Act, although other applicable law could still restrict it.

39. **Section 7(b)—Wind-down rules are absent.** The text does not address final reports, pending administrative proceedings, or continuing remedial duties when the Act expires. General federal savings law may preserve accrued penalties and liabilities, so sunset should not be described as automatically erasing past violations.

40. **Section 8—Six-month implementation window permits continued activity.** The prohibition and registration duties generally do not take effect for 180 days, allowing otherwise lawful mining to continue during that period. The bill also contains no implementation milestones to ensure the registry and enforcement arrangements are ready when the prohibition begins.
